units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay, you've turned a corner and the street opens up.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And now you're in it.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Stand somewhere near the middle and turn all the way around.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: This is the Grand Place. In Dutch it's the Grote Markt.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's a paved square, about sixty-eight meters by a hundred and ten, and every side is covered in decoration.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: I'm going to use the word "gold" a lot.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Do. Gilded statues, gilded cornices, gilded little ornaments on the top of every building.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Why is it all so ornate?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Because of who built it. This was the marketplace of a rich trading city, and the houses around the square belonged to the guilds, the associations of craftsmen and merchants.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The bakers, the brewers, the butchers, the tanners, the boatmen, the painters.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They competed with each other to have the grandest house on the square.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: A very medieval show-off contest.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Except it isn't medieval. Not most of it.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Here's the thing that surprises people.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Go on.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In August of 1695, during the Nine Years' War, a French army of about seventy thousand men under Marshal Villeroi bombarded Brussels, to draw enemy forces away from a siege at Namur.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They shelled the city for about two days.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Most of the Grand Place was destroyed.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Only the stone shell of the town hall and a few fragments of other buildings survived.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Wow. So what we're looking at...

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Was rebuilt in about four years.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The guilds put their houses back, under rules from the city council and the governor, in an exuberant Baroque style.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: So these golden facades are about three hundred and thirty years old, not seven hundred.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And still very pretty.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And a good example of what Brussels does.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It gets knocked down, and then it builds something even better to spite whoever did it.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Let's talk about the town hall.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: That's the Gothic building with the tall tower.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's the one old building left.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was built in stages, between 1401 and 1455, and its tower is about ninety-six meters tall.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And there's someone on top.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A golden Saint Michael, about two point seven meters tall, slaying a dragon.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He's the patron saint of the city.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: What you see is a copy from the nineteen-nineties.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The original is inside the City Museum.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Look at the tower carefully, I'm told.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Yes. Compare the two halves of the facade.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The tower isn't in the center.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's off to one side, and the building isn't symmetrical.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: There's a famous story that the architect found out and threw himself off the tower in despair, but that's almost certainly a legend.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Of course it is.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Let's turn around. Opposite the town hall is the building with the neo-Gothic facade, with lots of pointed arches.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's called the King's House, or the Maison du Roi.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In Dutch, the Broodhuis, the Bread House.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Bread house? Not very royal.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was named for the bread market that stood on the site.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was rebuilt in neo-Gothic style between 1874 and 1896, and since 1887 it's housed the Brussels City Museum, where that little boy is kept, in his original form.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the houses.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Have names. The guild houses each have a name, and often a symbol.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Number one is Le Roy d'Espagne, the King of Spain, which was the house of the bakers.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Number five is La Louve, the she-wolf, the archers' house.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Number eight, L'Étoile, the star, is a small and rather modest one, and number nine is Le Cygne, the swan, which belonged to the butchers.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: The butchers got the swan. Fair enough.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Next, a thing you might want to plan your trip around.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Ommegang. It's a costumed pageant held on the square in late June or early July, which re-enacts the Joyous Entry of Charles the Fifth and his son Philip in 1549.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: UNESCO recognized it in 2019.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the flower carpet.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Every two years in August, around Assumption Day, for three or four days, they cover part of the square with a carpet of nearly a million flowers, begonias or dahlias, about twenty-four meters by seventy-seven.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: A carpet made of a million flowers.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And the Grand Place has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1998.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And what about the t'Serclaes monument?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A short walk away. Remember, in 1356, the Count of Flanders invades and takes Brussels.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A citizen named Everard t'Serclaes leads a night raid with a small band of men, slips into the city, and drives the Flemish garrison out.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: A local hero.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And the monument, on the Rue Charles Buls, shows him lying dead.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Touch the bronze, the tradition says, and you'll have luck.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: You can see where millions of hands have polished it.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: I'll go with the luck.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Pause here for as long as you like.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Look up, look around, go into a café on the edge of the square if you want.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: When you're ready, we're heading north to a very different kind of place.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A covered arcade.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Walk with the Grand Place behind you, toward the little streets with all the restaurants.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: That's the Rue des Bouchers, the butchers' street.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Now it's lined with restaurants with menus on the pavement.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A word of advice. It's touristy, so look and keep walking.
